learn.title: Cloud models: public, private, hybrid (and multicloud)
objectives: Define the public, private and hybrid cloud models, plus multicloud.
List the strengths and trade-offs of each model: cost, control, scale, speed and responsibility.
Choose the right model for a workload from its business, regulatory and technical requirements.
Recognise the Azure services that support hybrid and multicloud: Azure Arc, Azure VMware Solution, Azure Local, VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute.
concepts: Built, owned and run by a provider such as Microsoft, and available to anyone who buys services. No CapEx, rapid provisioning and pay-as-you-go pricing, but no control over the physical hardware or facilities.

Cloud capabilities (virtualization, self-service, automation) dedicated to one organisation. It can sit in the organisation's own datacenter or be hosted by a third party. Maximum control, but the organisation pays for and maintains the hardware, and capacity is limited to what it has bought.
Public and private clouds connected so that workloads and data can move or interact between them. The organisation decides where each workload runs. Microsoft describes it as the most flexible model.
Using two or more public cloud providers at once, for example to use the best features of each, to satisfy acquisitions, or to reduce dependence on one vendor. The trade-off is more complexity.
Models are chosen workload by workload. One company can be public for its website, private for a regulated system, and hybrid overall.
Azure VPN Gateway (encrypted tunnels over the internet) and ExpressRoute (private dedicated connections that don't cross the public internet) link on-premises networks to Azure.
Projects servers, Kubernetes clusters and data services running outside Azure into Azure Resource Manager, so you can tag, monitor, secure and apply Azure Policy to them from Azure.
Dedicated VMware environments running in Azure, for moving VMware workloads without re-platforming.
Microsoft's on-premises infrastructure solution (formerly Azure Stack HCI) that runs virtual machines and containers on your own hardware and is managed through Azure.
terms: Infrastructure in facilities the organisation owns or controls.
Sending overflow demand from on-premises capacity to the public cloud during peaks.
Heavy dependence on one provider's proprietary services, which makes switching costly.
A requirement that data is stored in a particular geography.
Hardware dedicated to one customer, as in a private cloud.
Synchronises on-premises Active Directory identities to Microsoft Entra ID for hybrid identity.
services: Manage and govern resources outside Azure from Azure.
Run VMware workloads natively in Azure.
Azure-managed infrastructure that runs in your own datacenter or branch offices.
Encrypted site-to-site connections over the internet.
Private connectivity to Microsoft's network through a connectivity provider.
Replicate on-premises machines to Azure for disaster recovery.
Cache Azure Files shares on on-premises Windows file servers.
Discover, assess and migrate on-premises workloads to Azure.
examples: A start-up with no servers runs everything in Azure: public cloud.
A defence firm runs classified systems on hardware it owns: private cloud.
A bank keeps its ledger on-premises and runs its mobile app back end in Azure: hybrid.
A retailer uses Azure for analytics and another provider for e-commerce: multicloud.
A manufacturer uses Azure Arc to apply the same policies to its factory servers and its Azure VMs.
comparisons: Public: no CapEx, pay per use. Private: CapEx for hardware, and you pay for capacity even when it's idle.
Public: the provider controls the physical layer. Private: the organisation controls everything.
Public vs private: scale and speed
Public: near-unlimited capacity in minutes. Private: limited to owned hardware, so expansion takes procurement time.
Hybrid mixes private (on-premises) and public. Multicloud mixes several public providers. An environment can be both.
Arc manages resources that already exist anywhere. Azure Local is the on-premises infrastructure you deploy to run workloads locally.
VPN: encrypted over the public internet, quick to set up. ExpressRoute: private connection, more predictable performance, doesn't cross the public internet.
traps: Hybrid isn't 'two public clouds'. That's multicloud.
A private cloud can be hosted by a third party and still be private, because one organisation uses it.
Public cloud isn't inherently less secure. The provider secures the physical layer, and you secure your configuration.
Hybrid doesn't remove on-premises hardware; by definition some remains.
Choosing a model is per workload, not a once-only company-wide decision.
revision: Public = no CapEx, fastest, least physical control.
Private = most control, you buy and maintain the hardware, capacity is limited.
Hybrid = most flexibility, keeps existing investments, needs connectivity and consistent management.
Multicloud = several public providers, best-of-breed, more complexity.
Arc = manage anywhere from Azure. AVS = VMware in Azure. Azure Local = Azure-managed infrastructure on-premises.
